title: AI Agents in LangGraph
description: Learn to build stateful, multi-agent workflows using LangGraph. This course covers cognitive architectures, agent states, tool integration, and advanced patterns.

lessons.title: Introduction to AI Agents
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the concept of AI agents as autonomous entities driven by LLMs. It contrasts traditional prompt engineering with agentic workflows, emphasizing loop-based decision cycles over single-pass execution. The lesson also explores basic agent architectures, where the agent decides which tools to call and parses the results iteratively.
key_takeaways: AI agents use LLMs as their central cognitive engine to make decisions and use tools.
Agentic workflows rely on iterative loop execution (Reasoning-Action-Observation) instead of simple static pipelines.
Memory and state management are critical components of production-grade agent architectures.

revise_recall.question: What is the key difference between a standard prompt chain and an AI agent?
revise_recall.answer: A prompt chain executes a fixed sequence of steps, whereas an AI agent uses a feedback loop to dynamically decide the next action based on tool outputs.

revise_recall.question: Why is state management important in LangGraph?
revise_recall.answer: State management allows agents to retain context, memory, and execution history across multiple graph ticks and tool calls.

lessons.title: Building Stateful Graphs
lessons.summary: This module explores the core mechanics of LangGraph: Nodes, Edges, and State. Nodes represent execution steps or LLM calls, while Edges define control flow. The state schema acts as the single source of truth, updated by nodes via reducer functions. We walk through creating a stateful agent that queries a database and summarizes findings.
key_takeaways: Nodes in LangGraph are python functions that receive the current state and return state updates.
Conditional edges route the execution path dynamically based on the state contents.
Reducers define how state updates from nodes are merged together (e.g., appending to a message list).

revise_recall.question: What are the three main components of a LangGraph?
revise_recall.answer: State (the schema defining variables), Nodes (computational steps), and Edges (transitions between nodes).

revise_recall.question: How do reducers prevent state overwrites in list variables?
revise_recall.answer: Reducers append new items to the list instead of replacing the entire list, ensuring conversation history is preserved.
